q6.answer: A fences itself: a watchdog on A's database host renews a 30 s lease against the active-region record, and once the record moves to epoch n+1 renewals fail, so the watchdog sets Postgres read-only and stops it. The command waits 45 s (lease plus 15 s margin) before promoting B whether or not any API call to A worked, so A is already unable to write by then.

q7.answer: A small record {active, epoch, state, lease_expiry} in a separate strongly consistent store (a 3-node consensus store or managed equivalent) in a third region or provider, not in either database or DNS. The failover command writes it with compare-and-set at each step and reads it on rerun. A's watchdog reads and renews the lease against it. The final ACTIVE write is made by the command. I did not decide whether anything else, such as the app tier, reads it.

q8.answer: Rows marked running are replicated to B but their workers are gone. After promotion and before B's workers start, one idempotent statement sets them to pending and adds 1 to attempts, so they rerun. Jobs must therefore be safe to run twice, with idempotency keys on external side effects. Jobs enqueued or completed in the unreplicated tail are lost or rerun, and A's divergent tail is exported for manual reconciliation.

q9.answer: Rerun the same command. It keeps no local state, reads the record and checks whether B is still in recovery, then resumes at the first unfinished step. Going back to A is possible only before promotion (state FENCING or FENCED), through the documented abort that writes epoch n+2 with A active. A may need a Postgres restart because the watchdog may have stopped it. After PROMOTED there is no way back, only roll-forward and repairing B.

q10.answer: I did not design for this. The plan only says DNS has a 60 s TTL and moves to B after B is healthy, with no client-side behavior specified. A client with a stale cache would presumably hit dead or fenced A until the TTL expires, but I never decided or documented what it sees.

q11.answer: Loss is the unreplicated tail: writes A committed after B last received WAL, since replication is asynchronous. The lag gate (recorded replay lag of 30 s or less, or an explicit override) is only a floor, because it cannot see writes after B's last WAL receipt, so real loss can exceed it. The command prints the age of B's last WAL receipt as information. The 30 s RPO is a target the gate supports but cannot guarantee.
